description: How the longbow, the chevauchée and the Black Prince delivered England's greatest medieval victories.
content_html:
England’s Military Advantage

In the first two decades of the Hundred Years’ War, English armies achieved a series of astonishing victories against a larger and wealthier enemy. These victories were not accidents. They reflected specific tactical choices — above all the use of the longbow — and a deliberate strategy of devastating the French countryside to undermine French royal authority and force battle on English terms.

The Chevauchée: Burning France into Submission

The primary English offensive strategy was the chevauchée. English armies would ride through French territory burning villages, destroying crops, looting towns and killing livestock. The aim was not simply plunder — it was political. The French king was expected to protect his subjects. If he could not, his authority and prestige would suffer, potentially encouraging rival French lords or the common people to question his rule.

Chevauchées also had practical military benefits. They forced the French to respond, either accepting the humiliation of doing nothing or risking battle on ground chosen by the English. English commanders understood that their opponents’ heavy cavalry — French knights on horseback — were at a severe disadvantage when forced to charge uphill against massed archers in a prepared defensive position.

Key Fact

The chevauchée was both an economic weapon and a propaganda tool. By burning the French countryside, English armies demonstrated that Philip VI (and later John II) could not protect their subjects — striking at the king’s authority as well as his treasury.

The Battle of Crécy, 1346

The Battle of Crécy, fought on 26 August 1346, was the defining demonstration of English tactical superiority. Edward III positioned his army on a ridge near the village of Crécy in northern France, with his longbowmen on the flanks. When the French cavalry charged, the English archers unleashed a devastating storm of arrows. The French charged approximately fifteen or sixteen times but were repulsed each time with terrible losses.

The longbow proved decisive. Welsh and English archers could fire up to twelve arrows per minute, creating a density of fire that French armour could not withstand at close range. The French also deployed Genoese crossbowmen as allies, but their weapons were slower and less effective, and they were cut down or abandoned when the battle turned against France. Philip VI himself fled the field. The victory was complete.

The English longbow was typically made from a single stave of yew, around six feet long. It required years of training to use effectively — medieval skeletons of archers show distinctive bone deformations caused by drawing the bow repeatedly from boyhood. Its range of over 200 yards and rate of fire of up to twelve arrows per minute made it incomparably more effective in massed use than crossbows or the shorter bows used elsewhere in Europe. English law required free men to practise archery regularly, ensuring a large pool of trained archers available for military service.

The Siege of Calais, 1346–1347

Following Crécy, Edward III besieged the port of Calais. The town held out for almost a year before surrendering in August 1347. Its capture was strategically vital: Calais provided England with a permanent military and commercial bridgehead on the French coast, making future campaigns far easier to supply and reinforce. Edward expelled the French population and resettled the town with English merchants and craftsmen.

The story of the six burghers of Calais — leading citizens who offered themselves to Edward to spare the town — became one of the most famous episodes of the war. According to contemporary accounts, Queen Philippa interceded with Edward to spare their lives, and he relented. England held Calais until 1558.

Key Fact

Calais, captured in 1347 after a year-long siege, gave England a permanent base on the French coast. It was a supply depot, a military staging post, and a commercial centre. England held it for over two hundred years, until 1558.

The Battle of Poitiers, 1356, and the Black Prince

Ten years after Crécy, England won an even more dramatic victory at Poitiers. Edward, the Black Prince, led a chevauchée deep into France in 1356. Caught by a much larger French army under King John II near Poitiers, he chose a strong defensive position. On 19 September 1356, the French cavalry charged uphill against English and Welsh archers and were again devastated.

More dramatically, King John II of France was captured on the battlefield — one of the most valuable prisoners of the medieval era. His ransom was set at three million gold crowns, a sum so enormous that it strained French royal finances for years. The victory at Poitiers, combined with Crécy, demonstrated that English tactics were consistently superior to French heavy cavalry in pitched battle.

The capture of King John II at Poitiers gave Edward III enormous leverage. In 1360, the Treaty of Brétigny was agreed. France ceded full sovereignty over Aquitaine (expanding it significantly beyond its previous extent) and agreed to pay a ransom of three million gold crowns for John II. In return, Edward renounced his formal claim to the French throne — though this proved temporary, and the claim was revived when the treaty terms were not fully honoured. Brétigny marked the high point of English success in the first phase of the war.
exam_tip_html: On “explain a consequence” questions about the early English victories, avoid simply describing what happened at Crécy or Poitiers. Instead, explain the outcome and its impact: the capture of Calais as a permanent bridgehead, the ransom of King John II after Poitiers, and the favourable terms of the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360. For “explain a cause” questions about English military success, be specific: name the longbow’s rate of fire or the positioning of archers at Crécy — detail signals understanding, not just description.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The chevauchée was England’s strategic weapon — mounted raids that burned the French countryside, undermined the French king’s prestige and forced battle on English terms.
  • English longbowmen proved decisive at both Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), firing up to twelve arrows per minute to devastate French cavalry charges; Calais (captured 1347) became a vital English bridgehead.
  • The capture of King John II at Poitiers led to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), by which England gained full sovereignty over an expanded Aquitaine — the high point of English success in the early war.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the chevauchée as a military tactic.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for a simple identification, 2 for a developed feature. Example: The chevauchée involved mounted raiders burning crops and towns across French territory [1], undermining the French king's prestige by demonstrating he could not protect his subjects [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English victory at the Battle of Crécy in 1346.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature 1: Edward III positioned his army on a ridge with longbowmen on the flanks [1]; the massed archers repulsed approximately fifteen or sixteen French cavalry charges with devastating arrow fire [1]. Feature 2: The longbow's rate of fire — up to twelve arrows per minute — created a density of missiles that French armour could not withstand [1], and even Genoese crossbowmen deployed by France were outmatched and abandoned [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of English military success in the early Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (longbow, chevauchée tactics, defensive positioning at Crécy/Poitiers, experienced commanders such as the Black Prince) and explains it in depth with precise factual knowledge, showing how it led to English victories. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Battle of Poitiers (1356) for the French Crown.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains a consequence in depth — the capture of King John II and the subsequent ransom of three million gold crowns, which strained French finances; or the humiliation to French royal prestige; or the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) in which France ceded Aquitaine. Secure: Explains a consequence with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited development. Emerging: Vague point without factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the longbow to England's military success in the Hundred Years' War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance at the time (decisive at Crécy and Poitiers; gave England tactical advantage over French heavy cavalry; enabled much smaller English armies to defeat larger French forces) and over time (shaped English military identity; longbow archers remained central to English armies for decades; influenced how medieval warfare developed). Precise factual knowledge throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some longer-term reference. Developing: Describes the longbow without clearly explaining significance. Emerging: Limited knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The Battle of Crécy was the most important English military achievement of the early Hundred Years' War.' How far do you agree?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Crécy was the first great longbow victory, established English tactical superiority, and led directly to the capture of Calais (1347). Disagrees: Poitiers (1356) was arguably more significant — capturing King John II gave England enormous diplomatic leverage and led to the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) with its massive territorial and financial gains. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes events without evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple response; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the approximate maximum rate of fire of an English longbow in battle?
options: Two to three arrows per minute
Five to six arrows per minute
Ten to twelve arrows per minute
Fifteen to twenty arrows per minute

knowledge_checks.q: What was the main political purpose of a chevauchée?
options: To undermine the French king's prestige by showing he could not protect his people
To find food and supplies for English troops

knowledge_checks.q: The Battle of _____ was fought on 26 August 1346, when Edward III's longbowmen repulsed multiple French cavalry charges from a ridge position.
The Treaty of _____ in 1360 gave England full sovereignty over an expanded Aquitaine in exchange for Edward III renouncing his formal claim to the French throne.
Match each event to its date or significance:
right: 1356 — King John II of France captured
1347 — England gained a permanent French bridgehead

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Battle of Crécy fought?

flashcard_questions.a: A mounted raid burning French crops and towns to undermine the French king's authority and force battle.

flashcard_questions.q: How many arrows per minute could an English longbowman fire?
flashcard_questions.a: Up to twelve arrows per minute.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to King John II of France at the Battle of Poitiers?
flashcard_questions.a: He was captured by the Black Prince.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Battle of Poitiers fought?

flashcard_questions.a: Edward of Woodstock, eldest son of Edward III and England's most celebrated commander of the Hundred Years' War.

flashcard_questions.q: When did England capture Calais, and why was it significant?
flashcard_questions.a: 1347; it provided a permanent English military and commercial base on the French coast.

flashcard_questions.q: What did England gain from the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360?
flashcard_questions.a: Full sovereignty over an expanded Aquitaine and a ransom of three million gold crowns for King John II.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Treaty of Brétigny signed?
What material was the English longbow traditionally made from?
flashcard_questions.a: A single stave of yew wood.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did England expel Calais's French population after capturing it in 1347?
flashcard_questions.a: Edward III resettled it with English merchants and craftsmen to secure it as a permanent English base.

flashcard_questions.q: The chevauchée of 1356 that ended at Poitiers was led by which English commander?

glossary_terms.definition: A powerful bow made from a single stave of yew, capable of firing arrows over 200 yards with enough force to pierce armour; the decisive English weapon of the Hundred Years' War.
A mounted raid through enemy territory designed to burn crops, destroy towns and undermine the enemy king's prestige by showing he could not protect his people.
The battle fought on 26 August 1346 in northern France, where Edward III's army decisively defeated Philip VI using longbowmen in a prepared defensive position.
A port on the northern French coast captured by England in 1347 and held until 1558; a vital bridgehead for English armies in France.
Edward of Woodstock (1330–1376), eldest son of Edward III and the most celebrated English military commander of the Hundred Years' War.
The peace treaty of 1360 between England and France, by which England gained full sovereignty over Aquitaine and a large ransom for King John II of France.

hero_image_caption: Medieval longbowmen in formation, the decisive weapon of England's victories in France.
